strengths: The paper proposes a clear and potentially useful benchmark construction: turning diverse graph datasets into graph-alignment tasks with controllable noise, allowing GNNs to be compared on structural information rather than task-specific node/edge features.

The method is broadly applicable across synthetic, molecular, citation, and large-graph settings, and the benchmark results over multiple 1-WL MPNN architectures are reasonably extensive, with repeated runs and reported standard deviations.

The idea of reusing graph-alignment embeddings as positional encodings is original and interesting. The reported gains over Laplacian, RWPE, and SignNet-style baselines suggest that the pretraining signal may capture useful structural information.
The manuscript includes appendices with hyperparameters, dataset sizes, compute information, and a limitations section, which helps reproducibility and transparency.
weaknesses: A central assumption in dataset generation is not adequately justified: after randomly adding/removing edges, the identity permutation is treated as an optimal graph-alignment solution with only an informal 'high probability' claim. For real sparse graphs, molecular graphs, and graphs with symmetries or near-symmetries, this can fail or produce multiple optima, introducing label noise directly into the benchmark. The paper does not empirically verify optimality or quantify this risk.

The strongest claim, state-of-the-art PCQM4Mv2 performance, is not convincingly supported. Results are reported as validation MAE and compared to leaderboard models, but there is no official test-dev/test-challenge submission, no clear protocol matching, and only two runs. The reported 0.0337 MAE is extraordinarily better than listed methods while using only 2D structure and no bond information, so this claim requires much stronger validation and leakage analysis.

The positional encoding experiments may have transductive or preprocessing ambiguities. GAPE is pretrained on graph-alignment datasets derived from the same molecular dataset used downstream, but the paper does not clearly state whether validation/test graph structures are included in unsupervised pretraining or how splits are enforced. This matters especially for benchmark and leaderboard claims.

The baseline comparisons are not fully satisfying. Several baselines are weakened by omitting edge features and chemical information, SPE/PEARL are omitted due to OOM rather than tuned or scaled alternatives, and the comparison does not disentangle gains from the GAPE method versus larger pretraining/data access/hyperparameter choices.

The benchmark conclusions are somewhat overstated. The claim that anisotropic architectures have finer structural understanding, or that rankings generalize to downstream tasks with similar topology, is supported only indirectly by a limited set of architectures and datasets. The paper does not show downstream rank correlation between alignment benchmark performance and task performance across many models.

Some technical presentation issues reduce confidence: the loss is called binary cross-entropy but written as a softmax positive-label objective; the linear assignment equation appears to use inconsistent indexing; and several sections contain typos or imprecise statements. These are fixable but currently make the methodology harder to audit.

Reproducibility is promising but incomplete from the manuscript alone. The paper says an open-source Python package is provided, but the exact commands, package URL/version, dataset split generation, and full scripts for the PCQM4Mv2 state-of-the-art claim are not sufficiently specified in the text.

strengths: The paper identifies a real gap: many GNN benchmarks entangle graph structure with node/edge features, and a controllable structural benchmark could be useful.
The graph-alignment framing is conceptually natural for testing permutation-equivariant node representations, and the Siamese wrapper can in principle accommodate multiple GNN architectures.
The manuscript includes several datasets, repeated runs for the main benchmark tables, some compute/hyperparameter details, and an explicit limitations section.
weaknesses: The central dataset construction is not soundly justified. The paper defines a valid graph-alignment dataset as one where the provided permutation is an optimal solution, but the proposed construction only asserts that for small noise the planted identity is optimal with high probability. No theorem, empirical verification, or failure analysis is given for arbitrary real graph datasets, larger noise levels up to 30%, add-only molecular perturbations, automorphisms, or near-symmetric graphs. This directly undermines the training labels, the evaluation metric, and the benchmark claims.

The evaluation against a single planted permutation is problematic for graphs with automorphisms or multiple optimal alignments, which are common in molecular and synthetic graphs. A model could find an equally valid alignment and be scored as wrong, so the reported accuracies may not measure graph-alignment quality or structural understanding.

Several claims are substantially overstated. The paper says the benchmark “proves” anisotropic 1-WL GNNs have finer structural understanding and that rankings generalize to other tasks, but the evidence is limited to five locally implemented MPNNs under one Siamese training setup and no rigorous downstream correlation study.

The positional-encoding contribution is insufficiently isolated. GAPE is trained on graph-alignment datasets generated from the same graph distribution as the downstream task, but the paper does not clearly rule out transductive use of validation/test graph structures or analyze whether improvements come from task/dataset-specific pretraining rather than a generally better positional encoding.

The PCQM4Mv2 state-of-the-art claim is not convincing as presented. The reported validation MAE of 0.0337 is far better than listed strong baselines while allegedly using only 2D structure and no bond features, but the paper gives only sparse training details, two runs, no test/leaderboard submission evidence, no ablation separating GAPE from scale/training choices, and unclear comparability to leaderboard protocols.

Baseline comparisons are incomplete. SPE and PEARL are omitted due to OOM rather than evaluated under comparable feasible settings, and the molecular experiments use restricted transformers without edge features, making it hard to interpret practical significance relative to modern graph transformer baselines.

There are reproducibility and presentation issues despite the claimed open-source package: many exact architectural details are deferred to code, dataset generation validity is not checkable from the paper, some tables contain formatting/typo errors, and the loss is described as binary cross-entropy while the displayed formula is a positive-class softmax cross-entropy rather than BCE.

strengths: The paper proposes a clear and useful benchmark construction for evaluating structural understanding in GNNs via graph alignment. The formulation is well motivated: it avoids confounding topology with node/edge/task features and can be instantiated from both synthetic and real graph datasets with controllable difficulty.

The methodology is simple, extensible, and likely useful to the community. The siamese setup can wrap many equivariant GNN architectures, the graph perturbation procedure is easy to implement, and the benchmark can be adapted to domain-specific graph topologies such as molecules or citation networks.

The empirical section is fairly broad. The authors evaluate five standard 1-WL message-passing architectures over five base datasets and eight noise levels, with repeated runs and standard deviations. The analysis of an “optimal” noise regime where architecture differences are most visible is a nice practical insight for benchmark design.

The extension from benchmarking to Graph Alignment Positional Encodings is interesting and significant. GAPE performs competitively or best among several positional encodings on AQSOL, PCQM4Mv2, and ZINC, and the topology-transfer experiments provide useful evidence that the pretraining dataset matters.

The paper is generally well organized and readable. It includes algorithmic details, hyperparameters, compute information, dataset summaries, standard deviations, and an explicit limitations section, which helps reproducibility. The stated release of a Python package is also valuable if it is complete and anonymized.
weaknesses: A key methodological assumption is not fully justified: the generated graph pair is treated as aligned by the planted identity permutation when the perturbation noise is small, but the paper does not prove or empirically verify that this planted alignment is actually optimal for the arbitrary real-world graph topologies and noise levels used. If some labels are not true graph-alignment optima, the benchmark may partly measure recovery of the construction process rather than solving the stated graph alignment problem.

The benchmark evaluation is somewhat narrow relative to the claims. It mostly compares classic 1-WL MPNNs with similar parameter budgets; it does not include newer graph transformers, higher-order/expressive GNNs, subgraph GNNs, or specialized graph matching methods. This limits the strength of conclusions about GNN structural understanding in general.

The very strong PCQM4Mv2 state-of-the-art claim needs more care. The paper reports validation MAE values dramatically better than listed leaderboard models, but it is not sufficiently clear that all numbers are computed under the same split, feature setting, evaluation protocol, and submission regime. Results are averaged over only two runs for the scaled models, and no test-dev/test-challenge submission or uncertainty is reported for the headline SOTA claim.

Some claims are overstated. For example, the paper says the benchmark results will generalize to different tasks with similar topology, but direct evidence for this is limited mostly to molecular regression and positional encodings. The correlation between graph-alignment accuracy and downstream task performance is not systematically quantified across architectures, datasets, and tasks.

The GAPE comparisons are promising but not fully exhaustive or controlled. Several strong positional encodings are omitted from Table 1 due to OOM rather than compared under memory-matched settings, and the transformer architectures/hyperparameters may not be equally optimized for all baselines. This makes it harder to attribute the gains solely to the proposed positional encoding.

There are presentation and correctness issues that should be cleaned up. Algorithm 1 appears to contain an inequality/sign error in the BFS sampling condition, there are minor typos in tables and prose, and some appendix details are underspecified for independently reproducing the exact scaled PCQM4Mv2 result. The limitations section is honest but does not discuss the planted-label validity issue, which is central to the benchmark’s soundness.

strengths: The core idea of using graph alignment as a controllable, structure-only benchmark for GNNs is interesting and potentially useful, especially because the task can be instantiated on different graph topology families rather than only on a fixed synthetic generator.

The paper provides a reasonably broad empirical sweep over several 1-WL MPNN architectures, multiple base datasets, and multiple noise levels, and the observation that intermediate noise levels better separate architectures is a valuable practical benchmarking point.
The proposed reuse of alignment-trained node embeddings as graph positional encodings is a promising extension, with competitive results against several PE baselines on AQSOL, PCQM4Mv2, and ZINC.

The manuscript includes appendices with dataset generation details, hyperparameters, additional benchmark tables, and some discussion of limitations, which helps reproducibility relative to many benchmark papers.
weaknesses: A central soundness issue is that the planted alignment is not guaranteed to be the true graph-alignment optimum for most of the proposed datasets. The appendix acknowledges this and only cites an approximate Erdős-Rényi condition, then extrapolates it to molecular/social graphs without proof. Since the benchmark labels depend on this assumption, this materially weakens the validity of the reported accuracies.

Several theoretical claims are overstated. In particular, the WL hierarchy theorem/corollary only gives a bound based on indistinguishable node embeddings and does not establish a strict hierarchy of achievable performance for the benchmark in general. The paper also claims the task generalizes the WL test, but the formal connection is not developed rigorously enough to support that framing.

The empirical benchmark claims rely mostly on validation accuracy and visual/non-overlap arguments rather than stronger statistical testing, held-out test protocols, or sensitivity analysis over hyperparameters and dataset generation seeds. The claim that optimal-noise rankings generalize across all noise levels is asserted more strongly than the evidence supports.

The GAPE downstream experiments are suggestive but not fully convincing. Pretraining on the same dataset/topology as the downstream task may introduce transductive or distribution-specific advantages unless splits are carefully separated; this is not made sufficiently clear. Comparisons to PE baselines also omit some methods due to OOM rather than reporting controlled smaller-scale comparisons.

The adjacency reconstruction experiment is overinterpreted. A frozen encoder receives the graph structure as input, and reconstructing sparse adjacency from learned node embeddings does not by itself prove that graph alignment is a fundamental pretraining objective. Stronger baselines such as untrained encoders, Laplacian/RW encodings, degree/local-structure encodings, or matched-capacity autoencoders are needed.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the manuscript as provided: the abstract says the code is available but the URL appears missing, and some tables/text are malformed or inconsistent, including validation vs test wording and cramped numerical entries. The limitations section is honest but too narrow, omitting the planted-optimum assumption, possible split leakage, and benchmark validity threats.

strengths: The paper addresses a real need: GNN benchmarks that focus on structural reasoning rather than confounding node/edge features. The graph-alignment framing is a reasonable task family, and the ability to vary graph topology and perturbation level is potentially useful.

The manuscript includes a broad set of experiments across several base graph sources, multiple MPNN architectures, noise levels, and some downstream positional-encoding evaluations. Reporting repeated runs and standard deviations for several tables is a positive aspect.

The appendices provide some useful implementation detail, including dataset sizes, noise levels, model parameter budgets, optimizer settings, and additional results. The discussion connecting alignment to metric learning, denoising, and WL-style distinguishability is interesting.
weaknesses: A central assumption is not adequately justified: the planted identity/permutation is treated as an optimal graph-alignment solution for real graph topologies. The only theoretical support is an approximate Erdős-Rényi bound, yet the benchmark is mainly advertised as applying to arbitrary real graph datasets. If planted labels are not actually optimal, both training and evaluation targets can be wrong.

The empirical claims are substantially overclaimed. The paper says experiments “prove” an optimal task difficulty and robust architecture ranking, but the evidence is a finite sweep over selected models/datasets using an accuracy gap to the worst model, without statistical tests or a principled definition of optimality. Some conclusions about anisotropic models are also not cleanly supported across all tables and architectures.

The downstream GAPE evaluation is not convincing enough to support the stronger claims. Results are reported on validation MAE, the molecular setup removes edge features and therefore creates an artificial reliance on positional encodings, baseline fairness is unclear, some stronger baselines are omitted due to OOM, and the criticism of GPSE on ZINC is asserted rather than controlled experimentally.

The graph reconstruction experiment is weak evidence for “high-fidelity compression” or benchmark validity. The encoder receives the original adjacency to produce embeddings and a trained Transformer decoder reconstructs sparse adjacency matrices; accuracy is especially misleading under sparsity, and the experiment does not clearly rule out dataset priors or memorization-like effects.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the claim of an open-source package: the abstract says the source code is available at, but no URL appears in the extracted manuscript. Several experimental details remain underspecified, including exact splits, preprocessing, PE dimensions/baseline implementations, and model-selection protocol.

Presentation has multiple consistency and polish issues: table captions and text disagree about five vs. six datasets, ZINC appears in some appendices despite not being part of the main forty-dataset description, the PCQM4Mv2 total steps entry appears malformed, and the paper contains many grammatical errors. These issues make the already complex experimental story harder to audit.

The limitations and ethics treatment are inadequate. The limitations section is very short and misses major threats to validity such as non-optimal planted alignments, scalability of the N-by-N similarity matrix, BFS sampling bias/leakage for single large graphs, benchmark overfitting, and downstream evaluation limitations. The impact statement is boilerplate.

strengths: The paper proposes a useful and well-motivated benchmark for structural graph understanding based on graph alignment, with controllable task difficulty and applicability to multiple graph topology families rather than a single synthetic model.

The methodology is conceptually clean: the siamese GNN setup, planted correlated-graph construction, Hungarian decoding, and accuracy metric are easy to understand and broadly compatible with many equivariant GNN architectures.

The empirical study is fairly extensive for a benchmark paper, covering five base datasets, multiple noise levels, repeated runs, several standard 1-WL architectures, extended architectures, and higher-order GNNs in the appendix.

The paper provides promising evidence that the learned graph-alignment embeddings are not merely solving an artificial puzzle: GAPE improves transformer performance on molecular regression tasks and supports high-quality adjacency reconstruction.
The presentation is generally clear, with helpful figures, detailed appendices, hyperparameter tables, dataset statistics, and discussion of automorphisms and planted-alignment validity.
weaknesses: The central assumption that the planted permutation is the true optimal alignment is only rigorously justified for correlated Erdos-Renyi graphs and only heuristically transferred to real graph families. Since this assumption defines the labels, stronger empirical verification across all datasets/noise levels would be important.

Several claims are overstated relative to the evidence, e.g. that the benchmark results generalize to tasks sharing graph topology, that the task captures fundamental structural capability, or that an optimal noise level gives robust rankings. The evidence is encouraging but not conclusive.

The main benchmark uses validation accuracy rather than a clearly separated held-out test protocol, and the optimal noise level appears selected from observed sweeps. This weakens the interpretation of rankings as a benchmark standard.

The GAPE positional encoding comparisons are promising but not fully controlled: some competing methods are omitted due to OOM, hyperparameter tuning fairness is unclear, and GAPE benefits from dataset-specific pretraining on the same topology as the downstream task.

Reproducibility is partially addressed through claimed package support and many training details, but the manuscript text does not show an actual repository URL in the extracted abstract, and exact splits/seeds/preprocessing details are not fully specified in the main paper.

The limitations section is honest but narrow; it does not sufficiently discuss risks around benchmark label validity, post-hoc choice of task difficulty, computational cost for large graphs, or possible leakage/overfitting when pretraining and downstream datasets share the same graph distribution.
